<!-- The screenshots in figures/ were captured from run_app() with Demo mode
     left on, so they need no key and no network. Recapture them whenever the

Not every search starts in an editor. `run_app()` opens a local Shiny app that
drives the whole scopusflow workflow through a browser tab, from describing a
search to exporting the records, without writing any R. It runs on your own
machine, so your Scopus key never leaves it and requests come from your own
network. The app doubles as a way into the package itself, because it mirrors
every choice you make back as a runnable R script. Anything you can do in the
app you can also do from code, and the script panel shows you how.

This article describes the app without running it, since that would need a live
server, so the code chunks are shown but not evaluated. The screenshots were
taken from the running app with Demo mode left on, which needs no key and no
network, so everything they show can be reproduced on your own machine in a
minute.

## Launching the app

The app needs the suggested packages shiny, bslib and callr, and ggplot2 for the
plots. With those installed, one call opens it.

```{r}
library(scopusflow)
run_app()
```

By default it listens only on `127.0.0.1`, so it is reachable from your own
machine alone, and it opens your browser at the address it prints. Passing
`launch.browser = FALSE` leaves the browser to you, and `port` fixes the port
when you need a stable address.

## Demo mode

Demo mode is switched on when the app opens, so you can walk the whole flow with
no key at all. With it on, the harvest is simulated, the live terminal still
streams its per-cell progress, the tables and plots still render, and the Compare
topics tab still draws a figure. It is the quickest way to learn where each
control sits before you spend any quota. The records come from `example_records`,
the corpus of 138 real journal articles the package bundles because Scopus
records may not be redistributed, so every panel is exercised on real titles,
DOIs, journals and citation counts, and the by-year chart shows a real
publication curve with the shape the literature actually has. That corpus spans
2015 to 2024, which is where the year slider opens, and a year range reaching
outside it is drawn from the nearest year it holds, as the live terminal says
of each such year. Only the topic comparison is
synthesised, since it counts whole literatures, which no set of records in hand
can answer for. When you are ready for real results, paste your Scopus key into
the field at the top of the sidebar and switch Demo mode off. The key stays in
the running session and is never written into the generated script.

## Describing and sizing a search

The sidebar is where you describe the search. You enter your terms, choose which
field to search in, set a year range, and pick the level of detail. Partitioning
by year is recommended and switched on by default, because it keeps each cell
under the API's offset ceiling, the same reasoning behind a partitioned
`scopus_plan()` in code. Check size runs a cheap count first, the same one
`scopus_count()` performs, so you can see how much a query would retrieve before
committing to it. In demo mode it reports instead how many records it would draw
from the bundled corpus. The note answers for the search on screen, so it goes
as soon as the terms, the field, the years, the detail or the cap change. Check
size waits while a harvest is running, since the app runs one job at a time.
Max records per cell is blank when the app opens, so
the app sets no cap of its own, and each cell is retrieved up to the offset
ceiling of 5000 records. A number there caps each cell, or the whole search
when partitioning is off, which keeps a first look at a large search cheap, and
the script panel passes it as `max_results`.

It holds a Scopus API key field, a Demo mode checkbox switched on above a line reading "Demo mode: real bundled records, simulated comparison, no key needed." and the search terms "graphene supercapacitor". ## Fetching, with a live terminal

Fetch records starts the harvest in a background process, so the app stays
responsive while it works. The Live terminal panel tails the worker's output,
streaming a line as each year-cell starts, and a progress bar counts the cells
already finished. Cancel ends the background process at
once, which does abandon whatever cell was in flight. Every cell that had
already finished was checkpointed as it completed, and a checkpoint is written
to a temporary file and renamed into place, so a cancelled run leaves the cache
whole. Internally the app builds a `scopus_plan()` from your choices and hands
it to `scopus_fetch_plan()` with a cache directory and resume turned on.
Fetching the same search again in the same tab, after Cancel or a failure,
therefore resumes from the cells already checkpointed and spends nothing on
them.

Those checkpoints belong to the browser tab. Each tab keeps them in a temporary
directory of its own, removed when the tab closes. No search terms are left on
disk, and closing one tab never touches the harvest running in another. The
checkpoints also go when the app stops, so a harvest that has to outlast the
session, such as one stopped by the weekly quota, is the work of the script the
app writes. That script keeps its checkpoints under `scopus_cache_dir()`, in a
directory of the plan's own, and resumes from them each time it is run.

![The Retrieval panel part-way through a demo-mode harvest. A note reads "Demo plan: 10 year-cells; would draw 138 records from the bundled corpus.", and a label reads "Fetching cell 8 of 10" above a progress bar at 70%. The expanded Live terminal below shows eight lines, one for each cell the run has reached, each reading "Cell n/10: demo records for graphene supercapacitor" with its year, from 2015 to 2022.](figures/app-terminal.png)

## The reproducible code panel

The Reproducible code panel is what turns the app into a tutorial. It mirrors
every choice you make, the query, the field, the years, whether you partition by
year, and the Compare topics options, and rewrites a runnable R script as you go.
Change a control and the script updates at once, so you can see exactly which
argument each choice sets. The key never appears in the script. The panel notes
that it is read from the `SCOPUS_API_KEY` environment variable, so a script you
share carries the method but not your credentials. The script opens with the
version of scopusflow that wrote it, and one written in demo mode says next that
the records on screen were replayed from the bundled corpus. Its
`scopus_fetch_plan()` call keeps the plan's checkpoints in a directory of their
own under `scopus_cache_dir()`, named from the query and the years with a short
hash added. Scripts for different searches therefore never overwrite each
other's cells. The records are saved before anything is plotted, and the plot
is drawn only where ggplot2 is installed. With comparison terms entered, the
script ends with the comparison over the years the app compares. Download
script saves exactly what you see.

![The Reproducible code panel, holding the opening of the script the app has written from the choices in the sidebar. It starts with the comment "# scopusflow 0.4.0" and a demo-mode note saying that the records shown were replayed from example_records and that the script below is the live equivalent. Then come a library call, a scopus_plan() with the query, the years 2015 to 2024, the field and the yearly partition, and a scopus_count() to size the search. Last is a scopus_fetch_plan() whose cache directory lies under scopus_cache_dir() and is named graphene-supercapacitor-2015-2024 with a short hash added, with resume set. A comment records that the key is read from the SCOPUS_API_KEY environment variable and never written into the script.](figures/app-code.png)

## Reading the results

When the run finishes, the Results tabs come to life. Records shows a table of
titles, years, sources and citations. A line above it gives the number of
records the harvest holds, and says when the table shows only the first 25 of
them. A harvest that fails says why in the worker's own words. By year draws the
records per year through `autoplot()`, which traces the publications per year
when every record was retrieved. When a cap stopped a cell, the bars count the
records retrieved instead. The chart's caption says so, and so do a note in the
Retrieval panel and the search record. When the years reach the year of the
harvest, the caption also says that year was incomplete when the records were
retrieved. Top sources and Top authors tally the
most frequent of each with `scopus_top()` and `plot_scopus_top()`. Under the
`STANDARD` detail, the API sends the first author of each record alone, so a
note above the Top authors plot says that it tallies first authors, and choosing
`COMPLETE` gives every author. A harvest that matched nothing, or one whose
source titles or author names are all missing, says so in the tab where the
figure would be. Every figure is drawn by the same library functions you would
call from a script, so the app shows you nothing you could not reproduce, and
each carries a text alternative for a screen reader, naming what it shows.

![The Results panel with tabs for Records, By year, Top sources, Top authors, Compare topics and Export. The Records tab is open, with a line reading "138 records (showing the first 25)" above the first rows of a table of titles, years, journals and citation counts from the demo harvest. The first row is a 2015 article on all-solid-state symmetric graphene supercapacitors, published in the Journal of Inorganic Materials, with one citation. The rows below it are likewise real articles from the bundled corpus.](figures/app-results.png)

## Comparing topics

The Compare topics tab asks a different question from a harvest. It retrieves no
records at all, and measures instead how a set of sub-topics co-occur with your
search over time, as a share of it, with your search terms acting as the
reference topic. You enter comma-separated comparison terms, optionally pick one
to highlight, and toggle the stability band and whether record counts appear on
the labels. Each term needs one count request per year, and the reference topic
one more, so two terms over six years take 18 requests. The tab shows that
figure and advises fewer terms or years above 80. With Partition by year off,
the comparison covers the last six years. In demo mode the comparison is
synthesised so you can see the figure offline. A note under it says that its
counts are illustrative, since the figure's own caption names the Search API as
its source. With a key it calls
`scopus_compare_topics()` and draws the result with `plot_scopus_comparison()`,
the same figure the package produces, and a Comparison download saves the
underlying numbers as a CSV.

## Exporting

Every result the app shows comes with one-click export. The records can be saved
as an RDS file, as a clean DOI list, and as BibTeX and RIS for a reference
manager such as Zotero or EndNote, drawn from `as_bibtex()` and `as_ris()`, and
as a PRISMA-S search record in Markdown, drawn from `scopus_search_report()`. In
demo mode, that record names no search expression, plan or retrieval time. It
opens by saying that the records on screen were replayed from the bundled
corpus and that it describes no search that was run. The corpus carries the
phrase of the OpenAlex search that produced it, which is not a search anyone
sent to Scopus. The comparison can be saved as a CSV. Each button appears once
there is something for it to write, those for the records after a harvest and
the one for the comparison after a comparison. None of this contacts the API
again, because it works on results already in hand. Between the downloaded
script and the exported records, a session in the app leaves you with both the
data and the code that produced it.

## Beyond the app

Anything you can do in the app you can also do from code, but the reverse does
not hold. The app covers planning, retrieval and the trend, top and comparison
analyses, and the package goes further. `scopus_intersections()` counts how a
set of named concepts and their intersections overlap in the literature, and
`plot_scopus_intersections()` draws the result. `scopus_abstract()` retrieves
abstract text and richer metadata than the Search API returns, and
`scopus_corpus()` builds on it to give a harvest author keywords and structured
references for tools further downstream. When a session in the app has taken
you as far as it goes, the downloaded script is the place to carry on from.
